speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head X of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A vision for a future Singapore, one that we can all be proud of.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we journey towards that vision, it is perhaps helpful for us to look back, look inwards and also look forward.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In looking back, it is important to remind ourselves that home ownership has been and continues to be a key component of our national policy and a key pillar of our social compact with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have gone from Third World to First World, as one of the key movers of social mobility has been our provision of affordable, quality public housing for the vast majority of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our housing policy is one that is much lauded internationally, one that has allowed generations of Singaporeans to move up the social ladder.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Compared to many other countries like the United Kingdom (UK), Taiwan, Hong Kong and even Australia, just to name a few, the young there find it hard to rent a place, not to say afford to buy their own homes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: All these remind us of the purpose of development in our country: to provide better lives for our people.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This brings us to the opportunity to also look inwards, at a housing policy that seeks to be both practical and efficient, and also one that is compassionate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Flats for different people, different life stages, different incomes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Buy a home with your parents or stay near your parents, you get a grant.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: First-time applicants get a grant when buying a brand new or resale flat.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Rental flats have been made available to young married couples waiting for their new flats to be ready.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Flats for the elderly, to allow seniors to monetise their flats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are but some of the schemes that promulgate social equity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is something which we should rightly be proud of.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am also glad that the Fresh Start Housing scheme which allows families living in rental flats to be able to buy their own flats has taken off well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the same time, I feel for those who continue to live in rental flats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I refer to an opinion piece in The Straits Times dated 16 February this year, and it is titled, "The Housing and Development Board (HDB) should apply its own occupancy rules to rental housing".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They argue that this cap should also apply to those living in HDB's 1-room to 2-room rental flats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In their survey, they claimed that 15% of those living in rental flats had more than four household members.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They also state that overcrowding affects the well-being of children, family relationships and health.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have seen this first-hand and I am sure many of us in this House have residents like that, too.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I fully accept the Ministry’s stand that rental HDB flats are but an interim measure for families and they should be encouraged to move on to their own purchased flats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It would do wonders for the families living in these flats, particularly for their self-esteem and family relationships, if more can be done for them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What more can the Ministry do, in tandem with perhaps other Ministries, to do more for such residents and to give them that boost-up in social mobility?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are also our elders who are living in rental flats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Often, they end up sharing a small flat with a complete stranger, with no privacy whatsoever.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some even endure abuse from their flat mates, living uncomfortably in silence because they are afraid of having no other place to stay.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yesterday morning, the Ministry of National Development (MND) Facebook page also posted a link to an article on co-living.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is perhaps telling that the quote extracted for the post was this: "As it turns out, people do not really want to share bathrooms or bedrooms for that matter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But are fine perhaps with sharing kitchens, workspaces, gardens and the Internet".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, how does the Ministry, therefore, respond to the changing needs even within our rental populations, in this case, for our lower-income families and, especially for our elders?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another group of singles that the Ministry has made progress on is our younger singles.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since 2013, the Single Singaporean Citizen Scheme has also been enhanced to allow for direct purchase from HDB.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, while we continue to advocate strongly for more marriages and also strengthen parenthood benefits, society is evolving quickly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have come across many single Singaporeans who face challenges in securing their flats because we have fixed the age base as 35 years of age.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Younger Singaporeans are becoming financially independent earlier, and are marrying later, how then can the Ministry reiterate the reasons for setting the bar at 35 years of age, or will the Ministry consider reviewing this in the future?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, our policies perhaps are seen as compounding the difficulties of those already undergoing divorce, especially those who have custody of their children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While our HDB frontline staff do their best, it is perhaps time for us to take a better and closer look at how we respond to complex cases.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One of my residents saw me almost a year and a half ago.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She had full custody of her two children, but only for a limited time, and then joint custody after that.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She and her children were without a place to stay, moving from friend to friend, or renting short term from the open market.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I empathised with her and we worked on multiple solutions, yet each time that we tried, we were faced with a brick wall.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Replies were factual but offering no real solace for a mother desperate to provide a better environment for her two young children and a safe haven for herself.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Chinese, we have a saying, jing guan nan ban jia wu shi (清官难办家务事), even the most upright of judges will find it hard to settle family disputes, but try we must, and I think we can do better.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we strive for a compassionate system, it is also timely for us to look forward.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One of the topics that occupied the space last year was the issue of diminishing leases.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Along with those reducing leases, means that many of our flats – buildings and estate as a whole – are getting older.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, there is definitely a need for upgrading, renewal and rejuvenation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While the future excites us, we need the past to also remind us of where we have come from.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, amidst a future skyline, we need signs of our past to be preserved as our built heritage.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I spoke about this over the last two years of the Budget and hope that we can continue to do more.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore's first tallest residential condominium, Pearl Bank Apartments, will be meeting up with the wrecker's ball very soon.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, it is good to note that the developers have heeded the calls of heritage lovers and agreed to consider blending heritage elements into the new development.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What we can control, we do, but there are also clouds on the future horizon.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: According to the Climate Action Plan of 2016, sea levels are expected to rise, and with 30% of Singapore just five metres above sea level, what does this mean for our built infrastructures?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Part of this has been answered by the earlier Committee of Supply (COS) on the environment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To achieve our vision of a future city and home for all Singaporeans, we need the right professionals and know-how to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How else will the Ministry also grow the pool of local talents that we have in the fields of engineering, design, architecture and technology?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong, you can take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope more purpose-built flats, which take into consideration the needs of older generations, can be constructed.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When they move into such units, it can also free up the flats that they occupy to increase the supply in the resale market, hence, moderating the prices of the resale flats and increasing choices for those who do not have access to Build-To-Order (BTO) flats.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On top of the enhanced Proximity Housing Grant (PHG), would the Ministry also consider increasing the supply of multi-generation or dual-key flats?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such units facilitate intergeneration caregiving and bonding with grandparents helping to keep an eye on the grandchildren while the parents look after their elderly parents at the same time.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Most new flats will be built in new estates and to further encourage the elderly to move near their children, one of the best ways is to allow them to live together under the same roof.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Multi-generational and dual-key flats will provide the elderly with some degree of privacy and independence, while enjoying the benefits of proximity to their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Helping low-income and vulnerable families secure a roof over their heads is one of the most important things we can do.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many households are eligible but still on the waiting list?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will more flats be added to boost the stock of 58,000 units?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Ministry consider allocating more Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme (SERS) sites, which have been cleared but not immediately redeveloped, for such families?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Overcrowding can be a problem in many of HDB's public rental housing.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many of the subsidised rental flats have more than four occupants living together?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Ministry provide bigger households, especially those with children, with bigger units?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is feedback that the environment in subsidised rental blocks can be unconducive for children with security, cleanliness and noise pollution being the main issues.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To minimise such impacts on families living in these rental flats, what plans does HDB have to deal with these challenges?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How does the Ministry enforce regular maintenance and checks in this sector?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there plans to grow the pool of local engineers, technical and maintenance staff?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My concern arises from a number of incidents in recent years.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There had been a few cases of falling building parts, including cladding and other external features, although we have in place Periodic Structural Inspections once in a decade for residential buildings, and every five years for other buildings.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are limited to checking for structural defects.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Non-structural parts should also be checked, including exterior components, which undergo lots of wear and tear.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such checks are particularly important as the number of ageing buildings increase.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that the regulatory framework for the inspection of building facades is being reviewed.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When will the review be completed and the new regulations be implemented?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They occurred in different areas from Sengkang to Jurong West, Woodlands to Toa Payoh.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since these incidents have consistently taken place in previous years, HDB should take steps to minimise such problems through changes in the method of tiling and the type of adhesion materials used.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Compared to other regions, our temperature range is much narrower and thus, more predictable.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, these problems should be more manageable and preventable.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: HDB should also consider checking the quality of workmanship and penalise or even ban contractors whose work are not up to par.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another problem which plagues a number of buildings, from HDB blocks to commercial buildings, is lift operations and maintenance.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can we prevent the installation of poor-quality lifts in the first place?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are the long waits for repairs due more to manpower shortage or shortage of available replacement parts?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How severe is the shortage of qualified technicians and engineers here and what is the percentage of foreign and local staff?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, the deployment of new technologies and equipment, including drones, are ways to save on maintenance costs and improve safety.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on innovative measures being used or considered for enhancing the safety and integrity of our built environment?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The construction industry is one which employs a large pool of foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Because it is labour-intensive, the cost of construction, coupled with the rising cost of materials, has kept margins low for the industry players.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The need for the industry to adopt technology has also been a pressing need.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This can help companies to be more productive as well as to reduce their dependency on foreign labour.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This technology will enable architects, engineers and contractors to work together seamlessly, and allow them to anticipate issues and fix problems before construction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our overseas competitors from the United States (US), Britain and even China have been adopting this BIM technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, our contractors need to keep pace if we are to get a share of the business.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, how is the rejuvenating or remaking of our heartlands programme also linked to this?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, our economy has been changing at a fast pace and, as a result, there would be citizens who are caught in the fast-moving situation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some may lose their jobs and face financial challenges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A house is more than just a roof over one’s head.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It reinforces stability and rootedness in the community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, for families who had to sell their homes due to financial setbacks, this can be especially difficult and emotional at times.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Most of the time, their young children benefit tremendously from a changed environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, can I ask the Minister what is being done to help low-income and vulnerable families facing financial hardships?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can more be given through the Fresh Start Scheme, especially to help single divorced parents, get a slightly bigger flat than a two-room flexi-flat if they have more than three kids or more?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, you can take your two cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, will HDB build more larger flat types?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Flats with more rooms will reduce overcrowding for bigger families and facilitate procreation for those who aspire to have more kids.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many elderly residents have also told me that they would like to stay together with their children and grandchildren, but there is simply not enough space in current flat types.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some seniors also fear losing their autonomy and privacy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Dual-key units will allow them to have their private space to manage themselves.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can HDB waive the resale levy and give more help to senior citizens and retirees who apply to right-size to two-room flexi flats, as practised in the past for Special Account (SA) applicants?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are applicants who may not have sufficient funds in their Retirement Account (RA) nor cash to pay for the flat but, at the same time, they may not qualify for rental flats.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I would like to ask if there will be revisions to the terms and conditions for two-room flexi flats to enable more residents in rental flats to become owners.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, how many BTO flats have integrated two-room flexi rental flats for singles and other types of flats in the same block to promote community bonding and integration?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, our HDB rental flats provide a lifeline to low-income and vulnerable families which have fallen on hard times.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How many requests have been received from the applicants for a bigger rental flat due to the large family size and what is the success rate?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry consider allowing them to own a bigger flat with a shorter lease at an affordable price first and then allow them to top up later the lease once their economic condition improves?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For large families, this suggestion would assist to relieve overcrowding, which can aggravate tension among family members already in difficult circumstances.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Overcrowding is also highly unconducive for families with children and members, particularly the elderly, who are in poor health.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Chairman, home is a basic necessity for any individual and family.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Without a permanent shelter in which one can call their home, it is inevitable for individuals or families to feel much anxiety and stress.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Indirectly, this has broader implications on the society and can result in weaker social cohesion.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Over the years, MND had been introducing different options to cater for home ownership of Singaporeans at different stages in their lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This effort is encouraging and must continue to ensure everyone has a place to call their own.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, single parents with full custody of the children.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Divorce is unsettling for those who have to undergo the unfortunate situation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is not for us to judge the basis that triggered it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But for many who have children to care for, it is pertinent that they can provide a roof over the head of their young ones, especially if they are still schooling.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is increasingly difficult with small family units to assume that the divorcee can rely on their parents, siblings or relatives to help provide accommodation for them and their children.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And it is even more difficult for those who are placed at shelter homes where the distance to commute is unmanageable for the children of different schooling age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, seniors living in 5-room or executive flats with mentally incapacitated spouse.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While HDB encourages our seniors to downsize and monetise their assets, for some of them, this is not a choice.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I have encountered residents in such a situation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One has a wife suffering from severe dementia for years and they have no children.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: HDB has advised for them to rent their flat out.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But for those with a mentally incapacitated spouse, indeed, it is difficult to have another stranger or another family living in the same flat, be it for safety or emotional reasons.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, seniors living in short, as in less than 20-year leasehold private properties.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some seniors living in such properties are not well off.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They might have inherited the property while others bought it when they were much younger.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With a declining lease of the property, it poses a challenge for some to dispose of the property in the market.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While we cannot cater for every condition, we need to begin considering the support safety net for these seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Lastly, families where the spouse is a non-Permanent Resident (PR) and listed only as a flat occupier.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the earlier years, this is common for some family units to have only a single name listed as the sole owner of the HDB flat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Usually, the flat occupier happens to be the wife, who typically is the home maker.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Having lived in Singapore and raised their children here, some, to date, still remain as a foreigner due to different reasons.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As they aged, it becomes even more difficult for them to convert to a PR or Singapore Citizen.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The luckier ones may have children who have moved out to start their own family and are still able to support them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Others may not have any children or dependants.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the cases when the owner's spouse passes on, the plight of the living spouse will be quite tough.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Finding a place to live in will become a tall order for many, especially if the women have little or no savings, having not worked throughout their life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And this makes a concrete difference to Singaporeans every day.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But there are those singles who can only afford a 2-room BTO.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These singles still face a long waiting time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We must not forget that for every average waiting time, there are those who apply many, many times and are still unsuccessful.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, it is not about the lack of flats, but rather HDB processes that prolong the process.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, there should be a review of the whole HDB application process to see how it could be streamlined and speeded up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is the delay due to a shortage of manpower?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Or excessive paperwork, asking for information after information, or staff resigned and documents left in the tray unattended?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A resident told me that she applied for HDB Flat Eligibility (HLE) since February last year and still no news.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Then, the flats built in 1986 were 21 years old.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Today, the flats built in 1987 are 31 years old, a full decade older.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But they still do not qualify for HIP.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: About half of Nee Soon South was built in 1987.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, I can see that these flats need urgent repair.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: HIP will allow residents to do this at low cost and continue ageing in place.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many residents also asked why we did not replace rotting timber at the opening for the air-conditioners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is very expensive for residents to do it individually.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is economy of scale when done during HIP.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to reiterate the difficulties faced in some repairing or construction work in landed properties.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Not everyone is amenable to a neighbour's request to allow the workmen to carry out repair work, such as plastering on the neighbour's side.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider a law where residents are required to allow access to carry out certain types of repairs or construction work?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to move on to feeding of animals in housing estates.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is a growing trend for people to feed strays, especially stray cats, in housing estates.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But one has to exercise some responsibility when feeding these strays and clear up the food left behind.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why does NEA bother to spend valuable time and limited resources to monitor for two hours?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: By then, the feeders are nowhere to be found.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider introducing stricter laws on animal feeding in public areas?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I am glad to hear the setting up of the Infrastructure Office to tap on infrastructure opportunities in Asia.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After all, without a track record, how can they venture overseas?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I was told that some of the prequalifications called for Government projects are so onerous that none of the local contractors or consultants can qualify.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In cases like that, has the Government thought of how to involve the local companies instead of just having them as smaller players down the value chain?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, home ownership has been a core tenet of the nation ever since before Independence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Despite the Government's scheme to assist the elderly in home ownership, such as the Deferred Down Payment Scheme and the Temporary Loan Scheme for right sizing while having shorter leases for elderly owners, some basic flaws remain within our system, particularly for the elderly poor looking for the opportunity to own a home in their retirement years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The elderly poor enjoy the same level of subsidies as the poor and other age groups, but is likely to have little or less time to earn any further income.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those who work are likely to earn less than what they used to do in their younger years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those who are elderly, poor and single, the additional single's premium is yet another absolute hit to their life's savings that they can otherwise spend in their retirement years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The premium reduction of upwards to $5,000 based on their income level and length of lease upholds the rationale of the single's premium but reduces its impact for elderly poor singles who can then use their savings for their retirement.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Pritam Singh, you can take the two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, many residents look forward to HIP as it addresses long-time gripes, such as pipe leaks, ceiling leaks and spalling concrete, the last of which occurs due to corrosion of steel reinforcement bars over time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While this is a natural wear and tear process, many elderly residents, in particular, are unable to mitigate the problem with regular painting for financial reasons and a relative lack of mobility for some.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the course of house visits to homes where HIP works have already been undertaken, it is not surprising for residents to identify a re-occurrence of spalling concrete or a new occurrence in another area of the flat within a few years after HIP works are concluded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Although residents can request for the Goodwill Repair Assistance scheme, the cost for such repairs can come up to a few hundred dollars in some cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the HDB bear a greater part of the repair cost in view of the fact that the spalling concrete is fundamentally caused by the deterioration of the concrete floor slab in question?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This view can be correlated with the point that spalling concrete repair is deemed to be an essential improvement under HIP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the Ministry look to reduce the residents' component from spalling concrete repairs, particularly for flats that have already completed their HIP?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does it plan to call for a new HIP programme for flats built after 1986?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, can the Ministry share whether it is exploring how it can collaborate from a whole-of-Government perspective with agencies like the Smart Nation Office, the Public Utilities Board (PUB) and even the Ministry of Trade and Industry's (MTI's) initiatives under the Built Environment Industry Transformation Map (ITM) to incorporate future technologies with its future upgrading programmes?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is there a possibility of pneumatic waste disposal conveyance systems to be part of future upgrading programmes at older HDB estates?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, public rental housing remains an important feature of our public housing system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One of the reasons for this is to prevent overcrowding in HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are times when rental flat applicants share that crowded conditions at home make family living difficult, complicating already existing problems that are amplified in a low-income setting.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Part of the public rental flat assessment process includes an HDB enquiry into whether an applicant has other means of family support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Very often, for rejected cases, HDB seeks the cooperation of the Family Service Centre to address disputes between family members.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, not all cases can be resolved, with some issues particularly intractable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would HDB, in line with a tacit acknowledgement that overcrowding can affect the living environment, consider the number of individuals residing in a current place of residence for rental flat applicants as a factor for consideration at the point of application?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry share how many rental flat applications it has approved for applicants whose gross income has exceeded $1,500?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Png Eng Huat, you can take the three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, many residents living in older estates welcome the Home Improvement Programme (HIP) for good reasons.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The spalling concrete and water seepage problems I have seen in some of the older flats in Hougang are serious.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Next, many residents also wanted to do more for their ageing flats since HIP is going to disrupt their living environment for the next 10 days.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While residents can make arrangements on the side with subcontractors, some subcontractors may not want to do such improvement works for the fear of breaking any contractual terms under HIP.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I hope HDB would seriously look into redesigning the clothes drying rack offered by HIP.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The current one impedes repair and repainting work using gondolas and is an eyesore to see so many metal structures sticking out of a single HDB block.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Would HDB be open to tap on the polytechnics and universities to redesign the clothes drying rack for a change?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Unfortunately, these open spaces we knew and grew up with are shrinking in many new estates.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In its place are rooftop gardens and multi-purpose halls (MPH) about the size of two 5-room HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of the MPHs, unfortunately, were not designed with much thought and consideration for the very activities they were meant to cater for.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: At a recent briefing conducted by the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA), I shared with the team some of the observations and actual feedback from the ground on the MPH in Hougang Meadow, a relatively new estate with studio apartments.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: First, the MPH in Hougang Meadow is built on top of a car park.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: To do an event at the MPH, the only way to load and unload equipment and stuff for the event is via a narrow passageway connecting the sheltered compound to the multi-storey car park beside it.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Next, because of the proximity of the MPH to the nearby blocks, residents living on the lower floor can see the casket clearly from their windows whenever a funeral is held there.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In one wake that I attended, the bereaved family shared that there is no place around the MPH for the contractor to place portable toilets.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For a start there are no manhole discharge points.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Even using chemical portable toilets is an issue as these toilets need to be cleaned every day, and there is no way for the service crew to do it in a hygienic manner on the roof top garden beside the exercise area and children's playground.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The only place to locate the portable toilets would be under the block where the bereaved family lives.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is highly unusual for a wake at an HDB estate not to have sanitary convenience located onsite for bereaved family and friends who have to guard the wake throughout the night.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The design of the MPH also makes the sending off procession on the last day of the funeral very challenging.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The passage on the MPH at Hougang Meadow to the waiting hearse can barely accommodate the pall bearers and mourners.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They would also have to navigate the narrow passageway, pass the lift lobby at the entrance to the multi-storey car park and then make a U-turn down a deep ramp to a connecting car park and then to the waiting hearse at Level 1.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The alternative route to take would be a longer walk along the same narrow walkway cutting through other void decks and surrounding blocks and to a busy stretch of Upper Serangoon Road.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The same design issues are also present at Hougang Dew Court, another new estate with studio apartments.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But the saving grace is that the MPH is located on the ground floor.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I have shared the above concern with URA in the hope that future MPH design for new estates would take into consideration the various requirements of the activities these sheltered pavilions are meant to cater for.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As for the existing MPH, I hope HDB can look into correcting the design soonest as the void decks in these estates are too small and not suitable to hold any events like a funeral.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We have a strange situation in Singapore in that we have more lots than there are heavy vehicles.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But yet drivers are still facing inadequate parking lots in or near their estates.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The demand and supply of heavy vehicle parking lots on the ground generally follow the movement and turnover of drivers living in an estate and this is something hard to predict or control.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The then Senior Minister of State for National Development in 2016 had described ways to address the heavy vehicle parking issues.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The solution highlighted by the Minister then will take time to bear fruit.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In the interim, what can the Ministry do to help alleviate the issues faced by heavy vehicle drivers on the ground?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A driver told me he has to wait a long time for a vacant lot.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Each time when he works late, the chances of finding a lot would diminish greatly.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: He said he had to resort to illegal parking at times although he did so without causing obstruction or danger to other road users.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, take your two cuts together

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not only are the flats smaller than before, but the homes and buildings are also closer to one another now, thus it is not uncommon to meet residents troubled by stress from noise disturbances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2010, the Straits Times published an article on ideas to cut traffic noise pollution, where it was reported that some of the measures used included building multi-storey carparks between residential buildings and roads to screen out the noise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or has multi-storey carparks become themselves a source of noise pollution caused by the amplification of loud engines and screeching tyres?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has MND carried out studies to analyse the environmental and noise impact to nearby homes, or surveys of residents living in HDB blocks near multi-storey carparks?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government is taking big steps to shift towards prefabricated construction and generating lead demand via public sector projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some benefits include significant manpower savings and shorter construction times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we have a strong renovation culture in Singapore, with homeowners aspiring to personalise their new homes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With more HDB flats moving towards prefabricated construction, how will this affect home owners’ renovation aspirations?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will this create a price differential for resale flats in the future, given the strong renovation culture?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But housing support for such households is still quite lacking.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Currently, HDB exercises flexibility to help unmarried single parents with their housing needs on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This scheme, launched in May 2013, aims to provide assistance to divorced and widowed parents with children below 16 years old who may face challenges securing housing if they sell their matrimonial flat due to a divorce or death of a spouse.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As we are aware, unmarried single parents face similar challenges and struggles, if not more so, than the divorced and widowed parents.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, most unmarried single parents are of a young age and also a high percentage of them are mothers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some of these unmarried single parents are not getting support from their parents and other family members, due to their soured relationship and, as a result, some experience displacement.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I sincerely urge HDB to take further steps in their commitment to assist single parents by formulating a housing assistance scheme that caters to lighten the struggles of unmarried single parents.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And it makes matters worse when they have to worry about whether they have a home to live in after their divorce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In response to the Public Petition I filed, MND has stated that "a range of Government agencies work together to ensure that no child is without adequate housing, regardless of whether his or her parents are single or married".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the problem arises when parents do not have sole care and control of all the children and all the children are aged below 18 at the time of the divorce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They will need to get their ex-spouse’s consent to apply for subsidised public housing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This consent requirement is difficult since their relationship is clearly strained.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I feel the stigma from living in a rental flat is strong, especially when they seem to be isolated from the community, and I worry about how children brought up in this environment will feel and what the impact is on them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that there are existing HDB blocks where rental units are integrated with sold units in the same block, thereby integrating the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share HDB's experience with integrating rental units in the community and whether it has been beneficial for the children living there?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share whether HDB intends to build more of such blocks and, if so, when?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While there are still issues to be worked on, nothing and nobody is perfect, but we are definitely heading in the right direction and the collaborative approach has yielded much success for both our residents and the animals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, this really is not a cut per se.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I propose we do not cut their budget but hope that the Minister can consider increasing their budget so that the team that has done amazing work with very limited resources can do even more this year and can achieve even more progress.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I declare my interest as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of an international research consultancy that does work in agri-food and other areas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I moved an Adjournment Motion on indoor farming in Parliament in 2016, only a small fraction of the fund had been disbursed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I suspect good companies and projects do exist, as some have been highlighted in the media and in the Minister’s speeches.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Darryl David, you can take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, public housing is not just something that is a part of our national landscape.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a part of our national psyche.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With more than 80% of Singaporeans living in public housing and the fact that almost every Singaporean would have been to a public housing estate at some point in time, many visitors to our country are always amazed when I point out some of the more modern HDB blocks to them, saying that they look like private apartments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, such is the quality of design today that there are times when I myself cannot tell the difference between public housing and private condominiums when the two are side by side until I come much closer.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As much as the Government has continued to build modern, stylish and affordable new generation flats, it has also rolled out a variety of schemes and measures to enhance and improve the older flats at mature estates as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore imports more than 90% of the food we eat.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although our limited farming lands and fishing grounds have made it impossible for us to be self-sufficient in food supply, we should, nonetheless, support our local farmers to adopt new farming technology to enhance our food supply resiliency.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could AVA provide an update on the available schemes that our local farmers can tap on to develop their business?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will these schemes help us to meet our food needs and enhance our food safety and security?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that AVA has, in recent months, tendered out several plots of land to vegetable farmers to experiment with new farm and farming technologies.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Depending on the success of these projects, are there plans to help our farmers export their urban farming technology, or even other forms of Singaporean-developed agri-technology to the region and beyond?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From glow-in-the-dark trees, a solution that makes use of biomimicry technology and saves on street lighting, to the foot traffic electricity in London’s Heathrow airport, to parklets that have sprung up in urban areas to make city life more vibrant, much is being done all around the world for urban sustainability.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Parklets, for example, are very effective in increasing both green space and communal spaces in a city.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Essentially, parklets convert curb-side parking spaces into small scale public parks where people can sit and relax.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: People get the chance to meet friends for a chat while enjoying the city, thereby increasing community engagement.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, parklets replace parking spaces, reducing accessibility for cars and discouraging driving in the city, as part of a wider car-lite initiative.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are also initiatives like New York’s GrowOnUs canal in Gowanus.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Designed by Balmori Associates, a New York-based international landscape and urban design firm, the floating gardens act as sponges, filtering and cleaning water, as well as helping to provide wildlife with a safe habitat.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, home owners, from time to time, will redevelop the houses they own.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: URA and BCA have issued a very helpful advisory guide entitled "Be Good Neighbours" that provides useful guidance on how home owners should go about doing their rebuilding works.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is stated that due consideration should be given to neighbours, such as doing Pre-construction Surveys of properties nearby and asking a Professional Engineer (PE) to conduct an Impact Assessment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The guide understandably spends a few pages on Breakaway works, due to the potential difficulties with newly exposed walls and roof structures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While it would be ideal if all disputes between neighbours could be resolved through mediation, much depends on the nature of the problem and whether there are structural issues involved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is not my intention to criticise BCA, as I am aware of the good and efficient work it is doing in many areas.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The fact is that residents look to BCA to uphold standards in construction works.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It has inspired much imagination and plans and looks set to become an icon to shape new trends in land use, conservation, recreation and sustainability.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With its strong potential, the Rail Corridor will really become one of our brightest jewels in the western part of Singapore and in Bukit Gombak.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last year, we encouraged our residents to take part in the public consultation held by URA and the National Parks Board (NParks).

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Media reports have highlighted some of the feedback.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are looking forward to the many possibilities that the Rail Corridor will bring, especially for residents living in the vicinity.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As it develops the Rail Corridor, we hope that MND will take an integrated approach to land use, transportation and growing economic opportunities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, America’s Atlanta Beltline is one of its largest, wide-ranging urban redevelopment programmes.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The 22-mile loop is based on the former railroad corridors encircling the city of Atlanta.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It aims to ultimately connect 45 neighbourhoods and is now transforming the present landscape with multi-use trails and parks, modern streetcars or light rail transportation and affordable housing.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Beltline has also in its pipeline plans to conserve history, create jobs and contribute to public health.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I ask this because new residences or the introduction of commercial or community activities may release economic prospects that will energise the project’s offering.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, the historical significance and lush nature of the Rail Corridor make it an inviting spot for tourists to appreciate a lesser-known side of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For all this to happen, and key to the Corridor’s success, is accessibility and also good transport infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can this high-profile development be better served by a Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) station nearer than the current ones?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, will the residents living in the vicinity of the Corridor be able to easily access its trails or features?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, I just went to Summerhill Condominium last weekend.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The backyard of the Summerhill Condominium lies next to the fringe of the Rail Corridor.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, the residents from 20 over condominiums lying along Hillview Avenue hope that MND will allow a route to be constructed so that they can have a direct access to Railway Corridor instead of having to do a big detour.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are looking forward to the upcoming Coast-to-Coast Trail and also the new Nature Park Network announced by MND and NParks recently.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Other attractions that will be at the doorstep of the western part of Singapore and also Bukit Gombak residents are a heritage gallery at the old Bukit Timah Railway Station and food and beverage (F&B) outlets at the former station master’s quarters.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As MND plans the Rail Corridor’s access points, we urge MND and URA to give close attention to how it can be reached by more residents living around it.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Like the recent public consultation exercise has highlighted, the Rail Corridor is an important community space that the residents can share with fellow Singaporeans staying in the eastern part or even northern part of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, really, with good connectivity to the Rail Corridor, it plays a key role in its success.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are mindful of the need to also strike a balance between built development and nature conservation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, we hope that with an integrated approach and careful planning by MND and URA, this can be achieved, as shown by the success of other green spaces like New York City's High Line or the Coulee Verte in Paris.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With its unique qualities, the Rail Corridor in Singapore will not only enhance the quality of life but also create recreational opportunities for residents and many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It also has the promise of becoming a top icon emulated for its delightful combination of nature and biodiversity, for history and vibrant shared community spaces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The number of such management corporations in Singapore has been growing, in line with the number of strata units.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The large number of MCSTs would involve a large amount of resources and significant supply chains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The administration of such a large volume of resources by the MCSTs can have an impact on the output and productivity of industries involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Some attention should be paid to encouraging the MCSTs to streamline their operations, adopt digital technology where possible, and improve outcomes in general.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to know if there are programmes available for helping MCSTs to improve in efficiency and service delivery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Has the Ministry identified what the focus should be on in addressing the performance challenges of the large and disparate number of MCSTs that are currently in existence?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon, you can take your two cuts together, please.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, the Municipal Services Office (MSO) has been set up for more than three years now.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the time of the launch, many Singaporeans were happy to see that the Government was taking concrete steps to ensure that all municipal issues would be dealt with holistically.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In our digital age, users are accustomed to near-instant acknowledgement of messages and timely follow-up of any issues raised.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They expect to engage with providers and give them their feedback, positive or negative, in order to improve the overall product or service.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To keep pace with expectations, the launch of MSO was a timely and necessary step to improve coordination amongst Government agencies and ensure that issues are resolved expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Since the launch, MSO has not been in the public eye much and the general population may not know how it has performed.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Beyond its current scope, does MSO have any plans to expand or to streamline its services?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could the Minister also give us an update on how MSO has improved municipal service delivery and the management of complex municipal feedback submitted by its residents?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, the OneService app is the centrepiece of MSO's engagement with residents, serving as the one-stop shop for residents to report, track and receive information on any issues in their area.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It makes it simple for residents to report any issues in their neighbourhood with just a few clicks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just take a picture, fill in a few details, submit, press and voila, there you go!

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is an important step to create engagement with our residents, as we need everyone to take responsibility for the quality in their own environment.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, when I speak to residents, not many of them seem to be familiar with the app, and a good proportion have not even heard of it.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Given the potential benefits, could MSO give us an update on the uptake of the OneService App and are there any plans to further drive downloads and usage by residents?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister, beyond merely reporting of incidents around the neighbourhood, are there any plans to better utilise the platform to reach out to our residents?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Does MSO have any plans to leverage elements of Smart Nation and the Internet of Things (IoT), such as sensors on lifts or street lights, to identify issues even before residents encounter them?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Chairman, with the formation of NEA's Department of Public Cleanliness (DPC) in 2012, it subsumes the cleaning of public areas previously under the charge of various Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This is a great step towards better efficiency of municipal services.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: However, the cleanliness of public housing estates still remains with Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This is not sustainable, given the future outlook of an ageing population and the need to cut down reliance on foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Besides saving water, this frees up the cleaners to undertake more essential conservancy duties.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In fact, as corridors are mostly just used by residents themselves, they are unlikely to be very dirty if residents play their part by keeping their own surroundings clean.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: So, I am appreciative of Tampines residents accepting this new arrangement and doing their part.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Besides public cooperation, we need to think about how we can better organise the work that needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: So, speaking as Tampines Town Council Chairman, my experience tells me that most people cannot differentiate among the responsibilities of the different Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Unfortunately, the first finger that they point at will always be the Town Council.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I am not saying that the other agencies are not doing their work.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The fact is that various agencies are structured differently and we can do better by working together.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The Town Council staff are very much on the ground and able to supervise the work of the contractors.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In fact, we are also leveraging technology to help with monitoring.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: So, if we look at the public areas the DPC focuses on, they include roads, pavements, backlanes, walkways, footpaths, footbridges, overhead bridges, drains, waterways, vacant state lands, community parks and park connectors.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I do not expect the NEA officers to be able to check all these areas.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Some of these areas are also very isolated or longish narrow strips of land that adjoin public housing estates which I feel there is potential for the Town Council to help with the cleaning and supervision duty.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: While ownership and accountability run hand-in-hand, I wonder if we could just look at streamlining the deployment of cleaning resources in areas with a huge continuous expanse of public housing, for example, like Tampines.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Maintenance and repair of defects could still be handled by the respective agencies which own the land.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their comments and interest in MND matters.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MND's mission is to plan and build our city and home.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is a major undertaking and responsibility that span not just one or two years, but multiple years and even decades.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Singapore we have today is the result of hard work by those who came before us.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They master-planned our whole city, revamped our city centre, developed our housing estates.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Now, it is our turn to take Singapore forward.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must build a better Singapore for our children and future generations.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must plant the trees for them so that they can enjoy the shade.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we have a tremendous opportunity ahead of us to do this.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang himself affirmed this in his speech during the Budget Debate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have projects all over Singapore ‒ Changi Airport Terminal 5 (T5) in the East, Tuas Megaport in the West, we have the Jurong Lake District and the High Speed Rail, Woodlands, and the Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link with Johor, and the Punggol Digital District.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All of these projects would be coming on stream over the coming decade and they will help to strengthen our air, sea and land links.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They will also help to strengthen our digital connections so that Singapore can be a more connected hub for the region, so that our city can be more vibrant and more attractive to investments and talent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: More importantly, they will make Singapore a better home for our children and our future generations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To achieve these goals, our first priority is home ownership for Singaporeans because when you own a home, you have a stronger stake in the nation, and a greater sense of belonging.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is why home ownership remains a key pillar of our nation-building efforts, as Mr Alex Yam highlighted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government remains firmly committed to providing affordable and quality homes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we have tapered in a gentle way to ensure that there is sufficient supply.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we offered over 17,000 BTO flats last year and we will continue to maintain a steady supply this year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, we are watching the numbers carefully to ensure a balance in demand and supply for the longer term to maintain a stable and sustainable property market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Besides ensuring adequate supply, we remain committed to keeping prices affordable by pricing new flats below the market rate and having a generous subsidy in them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: One couple who have benefited are Mr Muhammad Fadli Bin Nordin and his wife Mdm Siti Diyana.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They applied for a 4-room BTO flat in Woodlands, received $15,000 in grants ‒ this is on top of the subsidised price ‒ and the monthly instalments for the loan are fully paid for using the Central Provident Fund (CPF).

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While waiting for their flat to be completed, they moved into a Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS) flat.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They benefited from the reduced PPHS rents last year, paying $900 instead of $1,100 per month.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They gave birth to a baby girl in the PPHS flat, they moved into their home in July last year, their new flat, and we are very happy that they have just welcomed their second daughter last week!

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We want to do more to help young couples like them with their first home.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is why we launched BTO flats with a shortened waiting time, not by compressing the construction, but by bringing it forward.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we build ahead and, therefore, the waiting time for the couples is shorter.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh suggested to further reduce the waiting time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will do our best and study how to do this, but please understand that it is not possible for us to do this for all flats, as some sites are just not ready for us to bring forward the construction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is physically not possible for HDB to produce instant flats to meet all of the demand.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, one way for those with more urgent needs is to buy from the resale market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we have taken steps to enhance the grants for resale flats.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We enhanced the CPF Housing Grant for resale flats last year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We introduced PHG in 2015 to help families live closer together and, this year, we enhanced the PHG.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And so, not surprisingly, we are seeing more first-timer families purchasing from the resale market, and I expect this to continue.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are also some young couples who decide to settle down early, sometimes when they are still completing their studies, perhaps when the males are still performing their National Service (NS).

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Take the example of Mr Gerald Sim and Ms Stefanie Mok.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Stefanie has just graduated; Gerald is still studying because he had to do his NS, so he is still studying.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are a young couple who have decided to settle down and would like to get married.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, they had been planning to buy a BTO flat since last year, but because Stefanie only started working in August last year, she did not have a sufficient period of employment to apply for grants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Young couples like them may find themselves delaying their flat application for one or two years and then waiting another four years for the flat to be ready.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think that is a bit too long a wait.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, if a young couple wants to settle down early and are confident they can finance the purchase of the flat, they can apply for the flat first.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They only need to pay half of the downpayment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We allow them to pay half the downpayment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The remaining half is paid at key collection.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The flat will typically take up to four years to build.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are also studying how we can further streamline processes to make buying an HDB flat much quicker and easier – I think the comments that Er Dr Lee Bee Wah made.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, we have already made several moves on this front.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have also made changes to our sales process and we started with the Re-Offer of Balance Flats (ROF) last year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Under ROF, all the unselected balance flats are pooled together in one common pool.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are not sorted out by flat types or by towns.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, applicants are put on a single queue and based on their queue number, they can choose any ROF unit that is available.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By doing so, we have been able to shorten the flat selection process.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A typical SBF exercise, as Er Dr Lee mentioned, takes about eight months.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It sounds very long, I can understand, but please understand that in a typical SBF exercise, there could be more than 100 different flat type and estate combinations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, you have more than 100 different queues to manage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our inaugural ROF exercise in August last year was a success, with more than 90% of the flats on offer being taken up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And just six months after the launch, about 400 families have already collected the keys to their new homes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will continue to learn from this experience to see how we can improve.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Another area that we are looking at is the balloting process for BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This used to be much simpler and faster in the past.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Member of Parliament would draw out two pieces of paper – one with the applicant's sales registration number, the other with a house number, and they match and this is it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: After they get this, sometimes behind the scenes, they swap.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because if you did not like it, you can go and swap, but that happened without our knowledge.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This was a simple process that used to happen in the past.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This was Mr Phua Bah Lee doing the balloting in the past.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that was how we used to do it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It was simple, it was possible, because the number of flats and applicants were much smaller.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Today, HDB serves more than 50,000 flat applicants annually, it has to manage across different priority schemes with ethnic quotas to administer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As a result, it takes about six weeks to work through the entire balloting process.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: HDB has to check applicants' eligibility, sort out the requirements of the various schemes and quotas and, ultimately, ensure that the ballot is fair.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: HDB has taken on this challenge and they are working through the processes and I hope they will be able to announce some good news before too long.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are also very mindful that children and parents would like to live near each other to provide mutual care and support and that is something that we want to encourage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: HDB offers various priority schemes, for example, the Married Child Priority Scheme (MCPS), Multi-Generation Priority Scheme (MGPS) and Senior Priority Scheme (SPS).

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These all help give priority to families to live closer together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh also suggested building larger flats so that families with more children can stay together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is, indeed, why we introduced 3Gen flats in 2013, and they had been well-received by home buyers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Chong Kee Hiong suggested increasing the supply of 3Gen flats.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So far, there is sufficient supply to meet demand, but we are monitoring the application rates closely and, if need be, we are prepared to build more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is also PHG, which I mentioned earlier, to help families to stay together and live near one another.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will apply to both the PHG for resale flats as well as the proximity-based schemes for new flats like MCPS and SPS, which I have mentioned earlier, from the May 2018 sales exercise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will give home buyers more choices of flats in neighbouring towns.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am very glad to see very strong support from Members for our efforts to encourage families to live closer together and, through all the schemes that we have, we look forward to seeing more families buy flats to live together or near one another for mutual support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While we help couples and families to settle down, we are also mindful that there is a diverse range of home buyers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are second-timers, elderly looking to right-size, singles, divorcees and single unmarried, unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are groups that various Members have talked about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
